newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Dresdner in danger of losing rating.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dresdner in danger of losing rating.

text.p: Dresdner Bank AG, the only remaining German private sector bank with a top credit rating from Moody's Investors Service, may be downgraded due to rising competition in the sector, the rating agency said on Friday.
Moody's said it had placed Dresdner's long-term senior Aaa ratings and its A bank financial strength ratings under review for a possible reduction.
The agency also said it might downgrade Dresdner subsidiaries Kleinwort Benson Group Plc, Dresdner Bank Luxembourg S.A. and Banque Internationale de Placement.
Dresdner, Germany's second largest bank, played down the move, saying it did not expect a downgrade to have a negative impact on the cost of obtaining fresh funds.
Investors also appeared unperturbed as Dresdner's share price closed Frankfurt floor trade up 0.50 marks, or one percent, at 53.90 marks, outperforming the share market as a whole.
Analysts were not surprised by the news after Moody's last year removed its triple A rating from Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest bank, and from Bayerische Vereinsbank AG, citing similar reasons.
The agency warned in January that further downgrades may follow as bank earnings were coming under pressure.

Moody's initiated the review because of a decline in Dresdner's traditional revenue sources amid "tighter competition, narrower lending yields, flatter loan demand and rising funding costs," it said in a statement.
While the bank was likely to remain among the financially sounder banks worldwide, its high cost structure and more modest core capitalisation may no longer justify the highest ratings, Moody's said.

A number of publicly-owned German banks whose capital is backed by state guarantees retain triple A ratings from Moody's. Among them are Bayerische Landesbank, Suedwestdeutsche Landesbank and Landesbank Hessen-Thueringen as well as state agencies like Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau.

Dresdner said it was surprised at the timing of Moody's announcement given that the bank will release initial results for 1996 on February 20. Most analysts expect it to report a 30 percent jump in net profit for the year.

Nathalie Grasegger, banking analyst at Bayerische Vereinsbank, said she was maintaining her hold recommendation for the shares. "Deutsche Bank's shares did not suffer after it lost its rating last December."

German banks, stung by spectacular corporate disasters in recent years such as the five billion-mark collapse of the Schneider real estate group in 1994, have become more cautious in extending funds and are competing more heavily for creditworthy clients.
That has squeezed their interest earnings, analysts said. In addition, the banks have been forced to offer higher interest rates on deposits as customers have become more demanding.

They are also labouring under heavy costs in their branch networks which they dare not reduce excessively for fear of losing business to savings and cooperative banks, major competitors in the highly fragmented German banking market.
These difficulties have prompted most of the big players to expand their investment banking, although that has made earnings more volatile by increasing their exposure to swings in financial markets.
But analysts said Moody's was underestimating the ability of universal banks to spread their risk.

"Even if we get more volatile results and dramatic earnings drops in bad market years, the banks' reserves and other sources of income are so high that it's an illusion to believe their ability to pay off liabilities may be impaired," said Konrad Becker, banking analyst at Merck, Finck in Duesseldorf.
